nodes.name: XFEL nonlinear Schrödinger equation
nodes.statement: The fundamental model for XFEL is the following nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{aligned} &i\hbar{\partial}_t\psi=\frac{1}{2m}(i\hbar\nabla-e\boldsymbol{\rm{A}})^2\psi+Ze\frac{1}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}|}\psi+e^2(|\cdot|^{- 1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi -\lambda|\psi|^\sigma\psi,\\ &\psi(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|_{t=0}=\psi_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
nodes.statement_short: First-principles NLS for an electron beam in XFEL: magnetic potential, nuclear Coulomb, Hartree and local Fock-type nonlinearity.

nodes.name: XFEL Schrödinger equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{aligned} &i\hbar{\partial}_t\psi=\frac{1}{2m}(i\hbar\nabla-e\boldsymbol{\rm{A}})^2\psi+Ze\frac{1}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}|}\psi+e^2(|\cdot|^{- 1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi -\lambda|\psi|^\sigma\psi,\\ &\psi(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|_{t=0}=\psi_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.label: eq000

nodes.name: Physical constants of the model
nodes.statement: Here $m_e$ is the electron mass, $e$ the electron charge, $Z$ the atomic number and $\hbar$ is the scaled (by $2\pi$) Planck constant.

nodes.name: Strength and power of the local nonlinearity
nodes.statement: The constant $\lambda>0$ measures the strenght of the local attractive nonlinearity with power $\sigma>0$, in particular $\sigma=\frac{2}{3}$ and $\lambda=3e^2\left(\frac{3}{8\pi}\right)^{1/3}$ for the local Hartree-Fock approximation.

nodes.name: Time-only dependence of the external field
nodes.statement: The vector field ${\boldsymbol{\rm{A}}}={\boldsymbol{\rm{A}}}(t)$ represents an external electromagnetic field, which we shall assume to depend on time $t$ only (not on position $\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}$).

nodes.name: Semiclassical rescaling
nodes.statement: Defining the semiclassical parameter $\varepsilon=\frac{\hbar t_c}{2m_ex_c^2}$ we obtain after rescaling \begin{equation*} i\varepsilon{\partial}_t\psi=(i\varepsilon\nabla-\boldsymbol{\rm{A}})^2\psi+\frac{c}{|x|}\psi+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi-a|\psi|^\sigma\psi \end{equation*} where $c=eZ\frac{t_c^2}{2m_ex_c}$, $C_1=e^2\frac{t_c^6}{8m_e^3x_c^4}$, $a=\lambda\left(\frac{t_c^2}{2m_ex_c^2}\right)^{\sigma+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Semiclassical parameter $\varepsilon$ and rescaled constants $c$, $C_1$, $a$ of the nondimensionalized equation.

nodes.name: Gauge/translation transform to the moving frame
nodes.statement: By setting \begin{equation} u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}) = \psi\(t, \boldsymbol{\rm{x}} + b(t)\) \exp\(\frac{i}{\varepsilon}\displaystyle\int_0^t{|\boldsymbol{\rm{A}}(s)|^2ds}\), \end{equation} where $b(t)=2\int_0^t\boldsymbol{\rm{A}}(s)ds$, one readily checks that $u$ satisfies the initial value problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\varepsilon\partial_tu=-\varepsilon^2\Delta u+\frac{c}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)|} u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u -a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u^\omega(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} where $u_0:=\psi_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift by $b(t)=2\int_0^t A$ and a phase factor turns the magnetic NLS into one with a moving Coulomb center.

nodes.name: Transformation (1.2)
nodes.statement: u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}) = \psi\(t, \boldsymbol{\rm{x}} + b(t)\) \exp\(\frac{i}{\varepsilon}\displaystyle\int_0^t{|\boldsymbol{\rm{A}}(s)|^2ds}\),
nodes.label: eqlenrd

nodes.name: Transformed initial value problem (1.3)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\varepsilon\partial_tu=-\varepsilon^2\Delta u+\frac{c}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)|} u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u -a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u^\omega(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.label: eq:fast-1

nodes.name: Oscillating displacement $b(t)=e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t)$
nodes.statement: Now we choose the scales $x_c, t_c$ such that $\varepsilon=1$ (thus relating $x_c$ and $t_c$ by $2m_ex_c^2=\hbar t_c$), since we are mostly interested in the fully quantum mechanical case, and we fix \begin{equation*} b(t)=e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t). \end{equation*} where $e:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is a smooth vector field, slowly varying in time.

nodes.name: Large frequency regime
nodes.statement: We consider the large frequency case \begin{equation*} |\omega|\gg\frac{{\rm sec}}{t_c}=\frac{\hbar}{2m_e}\left(\frac{{\rm meter}}{x_c}\right)^2\approx 5\times10^{-3}\left(\frac{{\rm meter}}{x_c}\right)^2. \end{equation*} and study the asymptotic regime $|\omega|\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Fast-oscillatory and time-averaged XFEL models
nodes.statement: In particular we shall investigate the convergence of solutions of \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega\\ &u^\omega(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} where the fast oscillatory potential is given by \begin{equation} V^\omega(t, x):=\frac{c}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t)|}, \end{equation} to solutions of the approximate problem (see \cite{xfel1} and Theorem 1 there) \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} with $\langle V\rangle$ is the time \emph{averaged} potential given by \begin{equation} \langle V\rangle(t, \boldsymbol{\rm{x}}):=\int_0^1\frac{c}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(t)\sin(2\pi s)|}ds. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fast model (1.4) with oscillating Coulomb potential $V^\omega$ and its averaged counterpart (1.6) with potential $\langle V\rangle$.

nodes.name: Fast-potential model (1.4)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega\\ &u^\omega(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.label: eq:fast

nodes.name: Fast oscillatory potential (1.5)
nodes.statement: V^\omega(t, x):=\frac{c}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(t)\sin(2\pi\omega t)|},
nodes.label: eq:fast-p

nodes.name: Time-averaged model (1.6)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u\\ &u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\big|_{t=0}=u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.label: eq:avr

nodes.name: Time-averaged potential (1.7)
nodes.statement: \langle V\rangle(t, \boldsymbol{\rm{x}}):=\int_0^1\frac{c}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(t)\sin(2\pi s)|}ds.
nodes.label: eq:avr-p

nodes.name: Averaged potential as weak limit
nodes.statement: We remark that \eqref{eq:avr-p} is well defined as the weak limit of $V^\omega$ defined in \eqref{eq:fast-p} in the space $L^\infty(\mathbb{R};L^{3-}(\mathbb{R}^3)+L^{3+}(\mathbb{R}^3))$, as $|\omega|\to\infty$ (see \cite{xfel1} for more details).
conclusions: \eqref{eq:avr-p} is well defined as the weak limit of $V^\omega$ defined in \eqref{eq:fast-p} in the space $L^\infty(\mathbb{R};L^{3-}(\mathbb{R}^3)+L^{3+}(\mathbb{R}^3))$

nodes.name: Physical size of $\omega$ in molecular imaging
nodes.statement: In molecular imaging (spatial characteristic scale of the order of magnitude of thousand nanometers, temporal characteristic scale of some femtoseconds), we compute $\omega\gg10^{15}$. Therefore it makes sense to investigate the asymptotic regime. We shall demonstrate later on that this is reached already for much smaller values of $\omega$.

nodes.name: Time-averaging theorem for the XFEL Schrödinger equation
nodes.statement: Let $0<\sigma<4/3$, $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, $u^\omega, u\in C(\mathbb{R}; L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$ be the unique global solutions of \eqref{eq:fast}, \eqref{eq:avr}, respectively. Then for each finite time $0<T<\infty$ and for each admissible Strichartz index pair $(q, r)$, we have \begin{equation*} \|u^\omega-u\|_{L^q([0, T]; L^r(\mathbb{R}^3))}\to0\qquad\textrm{as}\;|\omega|\to\infty. \end{equation*}
also_stated_at: In \cite{xfel1} it was shown that, under appropriate assumptions, the solution of \eqref{eq000} can be approximated, in the asymptotic regime $|\omega| \gg 1$, by the solution of an effective, time-averaged Schr\"odinger initial value problem.
assumptions: $u^\omega, u\in C(\mathbb{R}; L^2(\mathbb{R}^3))$ be the unique global solutions of \eqref{eq:fast}, \eqref{eq:avr}, respectively
for each finite time $0<T<\infty$ and for each admissible Strichartz index pair $(q, r)$
nodes.statement_short: For mass-subcritical $\sigma<4/3$, fast-model solutions converge to averaged-model solutions in Strichartz norms as $|\omega|\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Spectral convergence of time-splitting pseudo-spectral methods
nodes.statement: We have shown that these two methods have spectral convergency in spatial discretization \cite{BJM, HJMS, HJMS-2,HJMSZ}.
nodes.section: 2 Numerical methods for nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations 1.4 and 1.6
nodes.origin_citation: Bao, Jin, Markowich 2002; Huang, Jin, Markowich, Sparber 2007, 2008; Huang et al. 2005
conclusions: these two methods have spectral convergency in spatial discretization

nodes.name: Time-splitting spectral algorithm
nodes.statement: We solve \eqref{eq:fast} or \eqref{eq:avr} by a classical time-splitting spectral scheme as follows \cite{BJM, HJMSZ}: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{pseudo-spectral} method. Thus we can get the value of $u_1$ at new time $t^{n+1}$ by \[u^{n+1}_1=\(e^{-\mathrm{i}\Delta t |\xi|^2}\hat{u}_1^{n}(\xi)\)^\vee,\] here `$\wedge$' and `$\vee$' denote the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform respectively. Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, then we compute the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\] \textbf{Step 2.} We solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\Delta t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\,\exp\({\displaystyle-\mathrm{i} \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \left(C_1V_{Hartree}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})+V(s,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a\rho^\frac{\sigma}{2}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\right) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.origin_citation: Bao, Jin, Markowich 2002; Huang, Jin, Markowich, Sparber, Zheng 2005
nodes.statement_short: Strang-type splitting: free Schrödinger flow solved by FFT, then exact phase rotation by Hartree, Coulomb and local nonlinear potentials.

nodes.name: Step 1: kinetic step
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{pseudo-spectral} method. Thus we can get the value of $u_1$ at new time $t^{n+1}$ by \[u^{n+1}_1=\(e^{-\mathrm{i}\Delta t |\xi|^2}\hat{u}_1^{n}(\xi)\)^\vee,\] here `$\wedge$' and `$\vee$' denote the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform respectively. Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, then we compute the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\]
nodes.statement_short: Kinetic substep by pseudo-spectral FFT, then compute the Hartree potential.

nodes.name: Free Schrödinger flow by FFT
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{pseudo-spectral} method. Thus we can get the value of $u_1$ at new time $t^{n+1}$ by \[u^{n+1}_1=\(e^{-\mathrm{i}\Delta t |\xi|^2}\hat{u}_1^{n}(\xi)\)^\vee,\] here `$\wedge$' and `$\vee$' denote the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Solve $i\partial_t u_1=-\Delta u_1$ exactly in Fourier space over $\Delta t$.

nodes.name: Hartree potential via Fourier
nodes.statement: Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, then we compute the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\]
nodes.statement_short: Compute density and the Hartree potential by dividing by $|\xi|^2$ in Fourier space.

nodes.name: Step 2: potential step
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2.} We solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\Delta t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\,\exp\({\displaystyle-\mathrm{i} \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \left(C_1V_{Hartree}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})+V(s,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a\rho^\frac{\sigma}{2}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\right) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Potential substep: ODE solved exactly as the density is invariant.

nodes.name: Potential ODE
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2.} We solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the ODE with Hartree, external and nonlinear potentials.

nodes.name: Exact phase rotation
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\Delta t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\,\exp\({\displaystyle-\mathrm{i} \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \left(C_1V_{Hartree}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})+V(s,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a\rho^\frac{\sigma}{2}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\right) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $|u_2|$ is constant, integrate the ODE as an explicit phase factor.

nodes.name: Kinetic substep (2.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1, \\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: ts1

nodes.name: Potential substep (2.2)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}), \end{aligned}
nodes.label: ts2

nodes.name: Oscillatory Coulomb integral (2.3)
nodes.statement: \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(s)\right|}ds\equiv \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(s)\sin(2\pi\omega s)\right|}ds,

nodes.name: Gaussian regularization $\Phi^\eta$ of the Coulomb kernel
nodes.statement: For example, we could take \begin{equation}\int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(s)\right|}ds\approx \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t}\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(s)\right|}\)ds, \end{equation} where \[\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(s)\right|}\)=\(\frac{2}{\eta}\)^{\frac{3}{2}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}e^{-2\pi\frac{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}'|^2}{\eta}}\frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}'-b(s)\right|}d\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}'.\]
nodes.statement_short: Mollify the Coulomb singularity by Gaussian convolution of width $\eta$ before time-integrating.

nodes.name: Regularized oscillatory integral (2.4)
nodes.statement: \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(s)\right|}ds\approx \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t}\Phi^\eta \(\frac{1}{\left|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(s)\right|}\)ds,

nodes.statement: M(t):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2d\boldsymbol{\rm{x}},
nodes.label: eq:mass

nodes.name: XFEL model with external potential
nodes.statement: If we consider an external potential $V_{ext}\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)$ in the equation \eqref{eq000} \cite{Fri,MT}, we have \[ i\varepsilon\partial_t\psi=(i\varepsilon\nabla-A)^2\psi+V_{ext}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\psi+c\frac{1}{|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}|}\psi+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|\psi|^2)\psi -a|\psi|^\sigma\psi, \] by the same transformation \eqref{eqlenrd} and by fixing $\varepsilon=1$, we obtain the following equation \begin{equation} i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V_{ext}\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega, \end{equation} and its time-averaged problem is \begin{equation} i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V_{ext}\rangle u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u, \end{equation} with \[\langle V_{ext}\rangle(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}) = \displaystyle\int\limits_{-\frac{1}2}^{{\frac{1}2}} V_{ext}\left(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(t) \sin(2\pi s)\right) ds.\]
nodes.statement_short: Fast and averaged models (2.8)-(2.9) with an additional external potential and its time average.

nodes.name: Fast model with external potential (2.8)
nodes.statement: i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V_{ext}\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega,
nodes.label: ext-fast

nodes.name: Averaged model with external potential (2.9)
nodes.statement: i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V_{ext}\rangle u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u,
nodes.label: ext-avr

nodes.name: XFEL model with periodic lattice potential
nodes.statement: In particular, if we consider a case with an periodic potential $V_\Gamma\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)$ \cite{Fri,MT}, {\sl i.e.\/ } $V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}})$ is periodic w.r.t to a regular lattice $\Gamma$, \[V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}}+\gamma)=V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}}), \quad \forall \gamma\in\Gamma, \boldsymbol{\rm{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^3,\] the above two equations \eqref{ext-fast}--\eqref{ext-avr} become \begin{equation} i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V_\Gamma\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega, \end{equation} and its time-averaged problem is \begin{equation} i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V_\Gamma\rangle\(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\) u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u, \end{equation} with \[\langle V_{\Gamma}\rangle(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}) = \displaystyle\int\limits_{-\frac{1}2}^{{\frac{1}2}} V_{\Gamma}\left(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-e(t) \sin(2\pi s)\right) ds.\]
nodes.statement_short: Specialization to a $\Gamma$-periodic lattice potential, giving fast and averaged models (2.10)-(2.11).

nodes.name: Fast model with lattice (2.10)
nodes.statement: i\partial_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V_\Gamma\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega,
nodes.label: bloch-fast

nodes.name: Averaged model with lattice (2.11)
nodes.statement: i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V_\Gamma\rangle\(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\) u+\langle V\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u,
nodes.label: bloch-avr

nodes.name: Bloch-decomposition based time-splitting spectral algorithm
nodes.statement: We solve \eqref{bloch-fast} or \eqref{bloch-avr} by using the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based time-splitting method}, see \cite{HJMS, HJMS-2}. \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1 +V_\Gamma\(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\) u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based pseudo-spectral} method. Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, then we obtain the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\] \textbf{Step 2.} Then, we solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2\(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=u_1\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\Delta t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\,\exp\({\displaystyle-\mathrm{i} \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \(C_1V_{Hartree}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})+V(s,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a\rho^\frac{\sigma}{2}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=\left|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\right|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting with the periodic-lattice Schrödinger flow solved by Bloch decomposition, then exact phase rotation by remaining potentials.

nodes.name: Step 1: lattice kinetic step
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1 +V_\Gamma\(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\) u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based pseudo-spectral} method. Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, then we obtain the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\]
nodes.statement_short: Solve the lattice Schrödinger substep by Bloch decomposition, then compute the Hartree potential.

nodes.name: Bloch-decomposition flow
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1.} We solve the equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1 +V_\Gamma\(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\) u_1, \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} on a fixed time interval $\Delta t$, relying on the \emph{Bloch-decomposition based pseudo-spectral} method.
nodes.statement_short: Solve $i\partial_t u_1=-\Delta u_1+V_\Gamma u_1$ by the Bloch-decomposition pseudo-spectral method.

nodes.name: Hartree potential via Fourier
nodes.statement: Let $\rho(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2$, then we obtain the Hartree potential $V_{Hartree}$ by \[V_{Hartree}\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(t^{n+1}, \xi)\)^\vee.\]
nodes.statement_short: Compute density and Hartree potential in Fourier space.

nodes.name: Step 2: potential step
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2.} Then, we solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2\(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=u_1\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}. It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\Delta t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\,\exp\({\displaystyle-\mathrm{i} \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \(C_1V_{Hartree}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})+V(s,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a\rho^\frac{\sigma}{2}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=\left|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\right|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Potential substep solved exactly as a phase rotation.

nodes.name: Potential ODE
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2.} Then, we solve the ordinary differential equation \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2\(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=u_1\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\), \end{aligned} \end{equation} on the same time-interval, here $V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ is given by \eqref{eq:fast-p} or \eqref{eq:avr-p}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the ODE with Hartree, Coulomb and nonlinear potentials.

nodes.name: Exact phase rotation
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that in this step the density $\rho(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\equiv|u_2|^2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ and consequently the Hartree potential do not change in time, hence \[ u_2(t+\Delta t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=u_2(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\,\exp\({\displaystyle-\mathrm{i} \int_{t}^{t+\Delta t} \(C_1V_{Hartree}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})+V(s,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a\rho^\frac{\sigma}{2}(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\) ds}\) \] with $\rho(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=\left|u_1(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})\right|^2$, $V_{Hartree}(x)=\(\frac{1}{|\xi|^2}\hat{\rho}(\xi)\)^\vee$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the ODE explicitly since the density is invariant.

nodes.name: Lattice kinetic substep (2.12)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\, \mathrm{i} \partial _t u_1 = -\, \Delta u_1 +V_\Gamma\(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\) u_1, \\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: bd1

nodes.name: Lattice potential substep (2.13)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & \,\mathrm{i} \partial _tu_2 = \left(C_1V_{Hartree}+V(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})-a|u_2|^\sigma\right)u_2, \quad u_2\(t^{n},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\)=u_1\(t^{n+1},\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\), \end{aligned}
nodes.label: bd2

nodes.name: Bloch vs. standard pseudo-spectral method
nodes.statement: Certainly, if there is no lattice potential $V_\Gamma$, the above two algorithms are coincided with each other. But we must include the lattice potential $V_\Gamma$ when the interaction with laser or other lattice potenital are not eligible. We will see that the Bloch-decomposition based method is much more efficient in the case with lattice potential $V_\Gamma$ than the traditional pseudo-spectral method ({\sl cf.\/ } Fig. \ref{Fig012}-\ref{Fig013}), {\sl i.e.\/ } we could use much larger mesh size than the traditional pseudo-spectral method to get the same accuracy.
nodes.statement_short: Without lattice the two schemes coincide; with a lattice the Bloch scheme allows much coarser meshes for equal accuracy.

nodes.name: Convergence to the time-averaged model test
nodes.statement: Here we set the semiclassical parameter $\varepsilon=1$, $e(t)=(0,0,1)^T$, $\sigma=\frac{2}{3}$, $a=50$, $C_1=20$, $c=1$. We compare the time-averaged model with the fast-potential model for different values of $\omega$. We choose appropriate constants $C_1$ and $c$ to make the two potential components in the energy comparable.
nodes.label: ex1

nodes.name: Numerical convergence of energy and wave function
nodes.statement: From Figures \ref{Fig001}--\ref{Fig002}, we can see that as $|\omega|\to\infty$, the average of the energy $E^\omega(t)$ converges to the energy $E(t)$ of time-averaged model. The corresponding wave-function $u^\omega(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ also converges to $u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$ at least in $L^2$-norm. Figure \ref{Fig002} also shows the conservation of $E(t)$ and $M(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Numerically, averaged energy $E^\omega$ tends to $E$ and $u^\omega\to u$ in $L^2$ as $|\omega|\to\infty$; $E$ and $M$ are conserved.

nodes.name: Blow-up test (mass supercritical)
nodes.statement: Here we consider an example with $\varepsilon=1$, $e(t)=(0,0,1)^T$, $a=50$, $C_1=100$, $c=0.1$. We start the time-averaged model from a ground state for $\sigma=2/3$ ({\sl cf.\/ } plot (a) in Fig. \ref{Fig003}). Then we consider \eqref{eq:fast} with a mass supercritical power-type nonlinearity, i.e. $\sigma>4/3$, we analyse the blow-up of the norm \begin{equation} \|\nabla u\|_{L^2}=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|\nabla u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2d\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\right)^{1/2}.\end{equation}
nodes.label: ex2

nodes.name: $H^1$ seminorm (3.1)
nodes.statement: \|\nabla u\|_{L^2}=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|\nabla u(t,\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})|^2d\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}\right)^{1/2}.
nodes.label: eq:H1

nodes.name: Blow-up time decreases with $\sigma$
nodes.statement: In Fig. \ref{Fig003}--\ref{Fig004}, we can see that the blow-up time decreases as $\sigma$ increases.
conclusions: the blow-up time decreases as $\sigma$ increases

nodes.name: Averaged model accurate near blow-up
nodes.statement: Comparing the $L^2$ norms of the gradient of the wave-function for the time averaged model and the fast model in the blow up test we can see that they are very similar in the super-critical case ({\sl cf.\/ } Figures \ref{Fig005}--\ref{Fig006} and Figures \ref{Fig003}--\ref{Fig004}). They exhibit more differences in the subcritical case (see Fig. \ref{Fig007}--\ref{Fig008}).
conclusions: they are very similar in the super-critical case
They exhibit more differences in the subcritical case
nodes.statement_short: Gradient norms of fast and averaged models agree closely in the supercritical blow-up case, less so in the subcritical case.

nodes.name: Early-time impact of the Coulomb potential
nodes.statement: Furthermore, from Figures \ref{Fig009}--\ref{Fig009-1}, we can see that the Coulomb potential significantly impacts the wave packet at the early stage. This becomes particularly clear with slower blow-up and smaller frequency $\omega$.
conclusions: the Coulomb potential significantly impacts the wave packet at the early stage

nodes.name: Particle shot towards the oscillating field with harmonic trap
nodes.statement: Here we are interested in the patterns of interaction of the magnetic field with the particle, especially when a particle is shot towards the field, and scattered by it. We set $e=(0,0,1)^T$ in eq. (\ref{eq:fast-p}), and choose an initial datum of the form \[ u_0(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=e^{-4|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-(1,1,0)^T|^2+ i (x_1-x_2)}, \quad \mbox{ for } \boldsymbol{\rm{x}}=(x_1,x_2,x_3)^T. \] In this example, we add a harmonic trap potential \[V(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})=50|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}|^2,\] {\sl i.e.\/ } the equation in \eqref{eq:fast} becomes \begin{equation} i{\partial}_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega +C_1(|\cdot|\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.1.3 Interaction of the magnetic field with the particle
nodes.label: ex:shot

nodes.name: Fast model with harmonic trap (3.2)
nodes.statement: i{\partial}_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega +C_1(|\cdot|\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega
nodes.section: 3.1.3 Interaction of the magnetic field with the particle

nodes.name: Wave packet driven by the trap
nodes.statement: We can see that the wave packet moves under the interaction with the trap $V(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$.
nodes.section: 3.1.3 Interaction of the magnetic field with the particle
conclusions: the wave packet moves under the interaction with the trap $V(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}})$

nodes.name: Time-dependent polarization vector $e(t)$
nodes.statement: We consider a time-dependent vector $e(t)=(-1,-1,-1)\sin 2\pi t$ in eq. (\ref{eq:fast-p}), and an initial datum of the form \[ u_0(x)=e^{-4|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}|^2}. \]
nodes.label: ex:td

nodes.name: Weak effect of slowly varying $e(t)$
nodes.statement: As $e(t)$ is slowly varying in time, its effects are not very pronounced except when $e(t)$ is close to 0.
conclusions: its effects are not very pronounced except when $e(t)$ is close to 0

nodes.name: Interaction with a periodic lattice
nodes.statement: Finally, we consider a case with periodic lattice, {\sl i.e.\/ } the equation in \eqref{eq:fast} becomes \begin{equation} i{\partial}_tu^\omega=-\Delta u^\omega+V^\omega u^\omega+V_\Gamma\(\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}-b(t)\)u^\omega +C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u^\omega|^2)u^\omega-a|u^\omega|^\sigma u^\omega, \end{equation} and its time-averaged problem is \begin{equation} i{\partial}_tu=-\Delta u+\langle V\rangle u+\langle V_\Gamma\rangle u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u. \end{equation} We also take the initial datum of the form \[ u_0(x)=e^{-4|\boldsymbol{\rm{x}}|^2}. \] Here $V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}})$ is periodic w.r.t to a regular lattice $\Gamma$, \[V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}}+\gamma)=V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}}), \quad \forall \gamma\in\Gamma,\ \boldsymbol{\rm{y}}\in \mathbb{R}^3.\] For sake of simplicity, we choose \[V_\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\rm{y}})=\sum_{l=1}^3 \sin^2(\omega_l y_l), \quad \mbox{ for }\boldsymbol{\rm{y}}=(y_1,y_2,y_3)^T\in\mathbb{R}^3, \] with $\omega_1=\omega_2=\omega_3=2\pi$.
nodes.label: ex:pl

nodes.name: Fast model more peaked
nodes.statement: Certainly, the wave function of the fast model is more peaked than the solution of the time-averaged model.
conclusions: the wave function of the fast model is more peaked than the solution of the time-averaged model

nodes.name: Efficiency of Bloch-decomposition algorithm
nodes.statement: From these figures, we can also find that the Bloch-decomposition based algorithm is more efficient than traditional pseudo-spectral method in this case.
conclusions: the Bloch-decomposition based algorithm is more efficient than traditional pseudo-spectral method in this case

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the stability estimate
nodes.statement: The proof is indeed quite standard, as similar results are well known in the literature, see below for the references. The proof of stability of equation \eqref{eq:fast} with respect to perturbations of the potential is done by adapting in a straightforward way the local well-posedness result. For furhter details we refer the reader to \cite{Kato87}, \cite{Caz} Section 4.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the standard local well-posedness (Strichartz fixed-point) argument of Kato and Cazenave.

nodes.name: Stability of the fast XFEL model under potential perturbations
nodes.statement:
Let $V, 	ilde V$ be two potentials such that $V, 	ilde V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}; L^{ rac{3}{1+3\delta}}(\mathbb{R}^3)+L^{ rac{3}{1-3\delta}}(\mathbb{R}^3))$, $
abla V, 
abla	ilde V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}; L^{ rac{3}{2+3\delta}}(\mathbb{R}^3)+L^{ rac{3}{2-3\delta}}(\mathbb{R}^3))$, for some $\delta>0$ small. Let $u, 	ilde u$ be the solutions of the Cauchy problems  egin{equation*} \left\{ egin{aligned} &i\partial_tu=-\Delta u+V u+C_1(|\cdot|^{-1}\ast|u|^2)u-a|u|^\sigma u\ &u(t, oldsymbol{m{x}}) ig|_{t=0}=u_0( oldsymbol{m{x}}), \end{aligned}ight. \end{equation*} with the potential $V$ and respectively with $V$ replaced by $	ilde V$, and initial data $u_0$ and, respectively $	ilde u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$, respectively. Let $0<T<\min\{T_{max}, 	ilde T_{max}\}$, where $T_{max}, 	ilde T_{max}$ are the maximal existence times for $u, 	ilde u$, respectively. Then, for any admissible pair $(q, r)$, we have  egin{equation} \|u-	ilde u\|_{L^q((0, T); W^{1, r}(\mathbb{R}^3))}\leq C\pare{ \|u_0-	ilde u_0\|_{H^1}+\|V-	ilde V\|_{L^\infty_t(L^{ rac{3}{1+3\delta}}_x+L^{ rac{3}{1-3\delta}}_x)} +\|
abla(V-	ilde V)\|_{L^\infty_t(L^{ rac{3}{2+3\delta}}_x+L^{ rac{3}{2-3\delta}}_x)}}. \end{equation}
assumptions: $\nabla V, \nabla\tilde V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}; L^{\frac{3}{2+3\delta}}(\mathbb{R}^3)+L^{\frac{3}{2-3\delta}}(\mathbb{R}^3))$, for some $\delta>0$ small
